extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, and law students studying U.S. patent litigation and pleading practice
extracted.subtask_short: pleading and actions for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forms of action, pleading requirements, and substantive averments in U.S. patent infringement suits (declarations, venue, parties, proof of novelty/utility, marking, time of infringement, corporate liability, joinder, reissues, disclaimers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer liability for subordinate acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers of corporations should be bound to see that whatever they cause to be done is done lawfully, but it would not ordinarily be right to make them personally responsible to strangers for acts spontaneously committed by their subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers must supervise to ensure legality of acts they cause, but personal common-law liability for torts committed spontaneously by subordinates is not generally imposed; courts balance responsibility against unfairness of exposing officers to liability for all corporate torts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director collective liability when board authorizes infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors act only in a collective capacity; where an entire board unanimously orders an act which will constitute a patent infringement and the corporation's agents do the act, those directors may be held personally liable to an action for that infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unanimous board orders leading to infringement can expose each director to personal liability to prevent evasion by using an insolvent corporation as a shield. If only a majority orders infringement, minority voters are not liable unless they later ratify or are chargeable with gross non-attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority director non-liability absent ratification or gross non-attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement is ordered by a quorum or majority, members of the minority should not be held liable for the board's action unless they afterward adopt it by ratification or are chargeable with gross non-attendance upon meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being merely a director is not sufficient to render a person personally liable at common law for corporate torts; liability turns on participation, ratification, or culpable neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory personal liability of corporate actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Many States have statutes making officers, directors, or stockholders personally liable for corporate debts or liabilities under specified circumstances; such statutes are broad enough to cover liabilities arising from patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §721 Revised Statutes, state laws are rules of decision in common-law trials in U.S. courts; practitioners must consult controlling state statutes or special charters because statutory liability may be narrower or different than common-law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable liability of consolidated corporations for predecessor infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: A consolidated corporation is liable in equity for infringements committed before consolidation by each of its constituents if the property/franchises acquired from that constituent were of sufficient value, over paramount claims, to equal the profits or damages sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability here rests on equitable principles treating corporate property as held in trust for payment of debts; whether an action at law lies depends on state statutes, private acts authorizing consolidation, or corporate charters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of multiple patents in one action (single infringing thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plurality of patents may be sued upon in one action where the inventions covered are embodied in one infringing process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter; distinct devices that all contribute to a common purpose in a single structure may be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder is limited to situations where the accused product/process brings together the patented inventions into one infringing entity; separate unrelated patents generally cannot be joined in one law action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable joinder when defendant took license with non-infringement covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: When a defendant has taken a license under a number of patents and expressly agreed not to infringe any of them, a single suit in equity may be brought to enforce the agreement as to all the patents rather than separate actions at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an apparent exception to the general prohibition on joining unrelated patents in one suit—it's contractual/enforcement in equity rather than ordinary infringement joinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining action on plurality by proof of one patent's infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An action based on alleged infringement in one process or thing of a plurality of patents may be sustained by evidence that one of those patents was so infringed, though the others were not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff need not prove infringement of every joined patent if the complaint encompasses multiple patents applied to the same accused thing; evidence of any one may support the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining patent claims with trademark or unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: One action will lie for infringement of a patent and an infringement of a trade-mark where both were infringed together; a bill may also be brought for both patent infringement and unfair competition arising from the infringement, and federal courts have jurisdiction of unfair competition even between same-state citizens if acts constitute unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may be combined when facts overlap; federal jurisdiction for unfair competition may exist even absent diversity if grounded in acts related to patent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of action for patent damages and conformity with state practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for infringement may be recovered by action on the case; practice, pleadings, and forms in federal courts shall conform as near as may be to practice in state courts where the federal courts sit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleaders should be familiar with both common-law declaration requirements and relevant state code forms; courts have varied on whether federal pleadings must conform to common-law forms even in code states, so careful adherence to proper characteristics of a declaration is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action for fraudulently procuring a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An action at law lies for damages against one who fraudulently procures a patent for an invention which in fact was made by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct cause of action separate from ordinary infringement claims and should be pleaded when applicable (citation: Le Brocqce v. Childs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required parts of a declaration in infringement action
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper declaration should contain: (1) the title of the court; (2) the title of the term; (3) the venue; (4) the commencement; (5) the statement of the right of action; and (6) the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal components are essential to the common-law form of pleading in trespass on the case for patent infringement; federal practice may allow state forms, but pleaders should include these elements where common-law form is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue in patent actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue should be laid in the district, and division if any, where the action is commenced, regardless of the district(s) where the infringement was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory venue rules for the district of commencement; do not attempt to base venue on location of infringing acts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencement: party identification and citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: The commencement should state names of parties and capacity in which they sue or are sued; prudent to state nationality/citizenship (and for corporations, the state or sovereignty where created and exists); close by stating that the form of action is trespass on the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate party and citizenship allegations are important for jurisdiction and identification; although not strictly required in all instances, they help avoid jurisdictional defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of right of action: inventor identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of the right of action should contain the name, residence, and citizenship of the inventor upon whose application the patent was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These averments help identify the patent and the basis of title; include inventor details when they serve to identify the underlying application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averments as to novelty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty and utility of the invention must be put in issue by proper averments that include not only the general statement that the invention was new and useful, but also those details of the elements of novelty defined by statute (actual newness in this country and technical novelty throughout the world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not need to state the particular time the invention was made (i.e., prior to application), but include statutory elements of novelty and utility in the declaration to put these issues in issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment re: public use or sale (two-year bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement must aver that the invention was not in public use or on sale in this country for more than two years before the inventor's application for the patent; for patents applied for after 1897, the declaration must also aver that the invention was not patented or described in any printed publication more than two years prior to the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are statutory bars to patentability and must be negated in the plaintiff's pleading when relevant; include appropriate time-limited averments depending on the date of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying non-inventor patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee is neither party nor the inventor, it is proper to separately state his name, residence, and citizenship to fully and surely identify the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not legally required, including patentee details is prudent to avoid ambiguity about title to the letters patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to plead Patent Office application particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to state particulars of the application for the letters patent nor particulars of Patent Office proceedings, other than that the letters patent were granted upon the application of the inventor named in the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary detail about prosecution history in the declaration; a simple averment that the patent issued on the named inventor's application suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicating letters patent and profert
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration may indicate the letters patent in the language of the grant and make profert thereof; if so, it is not necessary to set out the specification verbatim because profert imports the patent by implication into the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pleading, reciting the grant language and making profert avoids lengthy verbatim specification recitals; for patents before/after April 11, 1902, include required formal statements about signing/countersigning/delivery as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading term and legal effect of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to state the particular term for which the letters patent were issued and to plead that the patent granted the patentee (his heirs or assigns) the exclusive right to make, use, and vend the invention throughout the United States and the Territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the patent term on the face of the patent and the territorial scope of the exclusive rights to establish the temporal and geographic bounds of the plaintiff's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading reissue patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the action is based on a reissue, the original letters patent should be set forth precisely as though no surrender and reissue had occurred; additionally, state the defect making the original a proper subject of reissue, that it arose from inadvertence/accident/mistake (not fraud), who surrendered it, and that the Commissioner issued a new patent and to whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reissue is prima facie evidence, these factual averments underlie the right to reissue and should be pleaded to put the issue properly before the court; avoid indefinite pleading when reliance is on reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading disclaimers and their timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclaimer has been filed, the declaration ought to state that fact and indicate its legal effect; it should also state that the disclaimer was filed without unreasonable delay because that fact is necessary to maintain suit on a patent requiring a disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers operate to amend and vary scope—plead them and their timeliness to avoid invalidity or procedural defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading patent extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent has been extended by a special Act of Congress and the suit is based partly or wholly on that extension, the declaration must state the legal effect of the Act and specially show the particular space of time covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions are statutory and exceptional; plead the extension statute and the precise extended term relied upon for the claim's time frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading chain of title when plaintiff is assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the plaintiff is an assignee or grantee of the patentee, it is safer to set forth all mesne assignments or grants down to him rather than merely state that the exclusive right came by assignment; the declaration must also allege ownership during the time of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title papers should be alleged by legal effect rather than copied verbatim; where letters testamentary or administration are involved, profert is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profert of title papers (when required)
rubrics_metrics.description: No profert is required of any assignment or grant of interest under letters patent generally; but if title papers include letters testamentary or of administration, profert of those documents must be made. Unnecessary profert will be treated as surplusage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include profert only where legally necessary to prove capacity or authority—avoid surplus copying of title documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking/notice averments (patented marking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration must state either that no one ever made or sold the patented article under authority of the patent; or that such articles that were made or sold had the word 'patented' with the day and year fixed thereon (or package marked when article cannot be marked); or that defendant was duly notified and continued to infringe after such notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These averments address the statutory marking/notice requirements affecting damages; plead the appropriate theory (marking or notice) to preserve claims for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of infringement (what to allege)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of infringement should allege that the defendant, without any license, did make, or did use, or did sell the subject of whatever claim(s) the plaintiff intends to prosecute, that the infringement occurred within the territory covered by plaintiff's title and during the time plaintiff held title, contrary to U.S. statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegation of any one of making/using/selling is sufficient to state a cause of action but will not support proof of the others; therefore a plaintiff should allege as many types of infringement as he expects to be able to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of infringement pleading and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The time of infringement should be stated by alleging a specified day and divers other days between that day and some later date; plaintiff cannot prove infringement outside times specified in the declaration. It is not necessary to plead the six-year statutory period; lack of infringement within the statutory period is a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All infringements complained of must have occurred after plaintiff obtained title and before the action began. If plaintiff acquired prior causes of action by assignment for pre-assignment infringements, a separate action in the name of the owner at the time is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple infringements and separate actions for pre-assignment acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Several infringements of the same patent committed at different times by the same infringer may be sued in several actions or within one action (subject to pleading the time limits); but infringements that accrued before an assignee's purchase require a separate action brought in the name of the person who owned the patent when those infringements accrued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully align the time periods pleaded with the plaintiff's period of ownership to avoid defective pleading or missing claims.
